claim: Variant counts analyzed by sequencing before and after the pre-selection amplification step were correlated, consistent with minimal to no selection prior to induction with β-estradiol.
source: Variant counts analyzed by sequencing before and after the pre-selection amplification step were correlated, consistent with minimal to no selection prior to induction with β-estradiol (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is a result validating the experimental approach.

claim: For the fluorescent screens, cells were incubated with β-estradiol at 125 nM for the time required for WT Mpro to achieve full reporter activity (1.5 hr for the FRET screen and 6 hr for the TF screen).
source: For the fluorescent screens, the cells were incubated with β-estradiol at the concentration determined to limit Mpro toxicity (125 nM) for the time required for WT Mpro to achieve full reporter activity (1.5 hr for the FRET screen and 6 hr for the TF screen).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for the fluorescent screens.

claim: For the growth screen, cells were incubated with 2 µM β-estradiol.
source: For the growth screen, cells were incubated with a higher concentration of β-estradiol determined to slow yeast growth (2 µM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for the growth screen.

claim: For the TF and FRET screens, the functional score of each mutant was calculated as the fraction of the mutant in the cut population relative to its fraction in both populations.
source: For the TF and FRET screens, the functional score of each mutant was calculated as the fraction of the mutant in the cut population relative to its fraction in both populations.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating functional scores.

claim: For the growth screen, the functional score was calculated as the fraction of the mutant at the 0 hr time point relative to the fraction in the 0 hr and 16 hr time points.
source: For the growth screen, the functional score was calculated as the fraction of the mutant at the 0 hr time point relative to the fraction in the 0 hr and 16 hr time points.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating functional scores.

claim: Functional scores were normalized setting the score for the average WT Mpro barcode as 1 and the average stop codon as 0.
source: We normalized the functional scores in all three screens to facilitate comparisons, setting the score for the average WT Mpro barcode as 1 and the average stop codon as 0 (see Figure 2—source data 1 for all functional scores).
evidence: This describes the normalization method for functional scores.

claim: Functional scores between replicates were strongly correlated (R2>0.98 for all three screens).
source: Functional scores between replicates were strongly correlated (R2>0.98 for all three screens, Figure 2a) and we could clearly distinguish between functional scores for WT Mpro and those containing stop codons (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a result demonstrating the reproducibility of the screens.

claim: WT Mpro and stop codons could be clearly distinguished based on functional scores.
source: Functional scores between replicates were strongly correlated (R2>0.98 for all three screens, Figure 2a) and we could clearly distinguish between functional scores for WT Mpro and those containing stop codons (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a result demonstrating the validity of the functional scores.

claim: There was a narrow distribution of functional scores for stop codons in all three screens across the Mpro sequence except at the last seven positions (amino acids 300–306).
source: There was a narrow distribution of functional scores for stop codons in all the three screens across the Mpro sequence except at the last seven positions (amino acids 300–306) (Figure 2c), supporting previous experiments showing that these residues are dispensable for Mpro activity and the importance of residue Q299 for Mpro function (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a result that is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Residues 300–306 at the C-terminus are dispensable for Mpro activity.
source: There was a narrow distribution of functional scores for stop codons in all the three screens across the Mpro sequence except at the last seven positions (amino acids 300–306) (Figure 2c), supporting previous experiments showing that these residues are dispensable for Mpro activity and the importance of residue Q299 for Mpro function (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Residue Q299 is important for Mpro function.
source: There was a narrow distribution of functional scores for stop codons in all the three screens across the Mpro sequence except at the last seven positions (amino acids 300–306) (Figure 2c), supporting previous experiments showing that these residues are dispensable for Mpro activity and the importance of residue Q299 for Mpro function (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Comparing the average functional score at each position between the three screens shows a strong correlation.
source: Comparing the average functional score at each position (a measure of mutational sensitivity) between the three screens shows a strong correlation (Figure 4a–c).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the three screens.

claim: The average defective mutation in the growth screen is more exaggerated than that in the fluorescent-based screens.
source: The principal differences lie in the sensitivity of the screens to mutation, with the average defective mutation in the growth screen being more exaggerated than that in the fluorescent-based screens (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the screens.

claim: The scores in the growth screen are likely integrating cutting efficiency over a diverse set of cleavages sites which may contribute to this screen's increased sensitivity to mutation.
source: The scores in the growth screen are likely integrating cutting efficiency over a diverse set of cleavages sites which may contribute to this screen's increased sensitivity to mutation.
evidence: This is an inference about why the growth screen is more sensitive.

claim: There are striking correlations in the mutational patterns of Mpro across all three screens.
source: Despite these differences, there are striking correlations in the mutational patterns of Mpro across all three screens as can be visualized in the heatmap of average scores per position and when mapped to Mpro's structure (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the three screens.

claim: The similarities between the three screens indicate that they are reporting the same fundamental biophysical and biochemical constraints of the protein.
source: These similarities indicate that the three screens are reporting the same fundamental biophysical and biochemical constraints of the protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between screens.

claim: Mutating the residues of the catalytic dyad, C145 and H41, inactivates the protease both in the screens and in in vitro biochemical assays.
source: For example, mutating the residues of the catalytic dyad, C145 and H41, inactivates the protease both in our screen and in in vitro biochemical assays as expected (Hegyi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation and validates the screens against known biology.

claim: In vitro assays have shown that residues at the dimer interface including S10, G11, and E14 are essential for SARS-CoV-1 Mpro dimerization and function.
source: Additionally, in vitro assays have shown that residues at the dimer interface including S10, G11, and E14 are essential for SARS-CoV-1 Mpro dimerization and function (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mutations at S10, G11, and E14 are deleterious to Mpro function in the screens.
source: Mutations at these residues are also deleterious to Mpro function in our screen.
evidence: This is a result that validates the screens against known biology.

claim: Because of the high sequence and functional similarities between SARS-CoV-1 and CoV-2 Mpro, the majority of the mutational analyses performed previously on SARS-CoV-1 Mpro are expected to be valid for SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
source: Because of the high sequence and functional similarities between SARS-CoV-1 and CoV-2 Mpro, we expect that the majority of the mutational analyses performed previously on SARS-CoV-1 Mpro will be valid for SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity.

claim: The growth screen measurements exhibited a linear pattern with relative catalytic rates previously reported for individual variants.
source: The growth screen measurements exhibited a linear pattern with relative catalytic rates previously reported for individual variants (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a result from comparing functional scores to published catalytic rates.

claim: The TF screen results showed a non-linear pattern with catalytic rates, reminiscent of a binding equation.
source: In contrast, the TF screen results showed a non-linear pattern, reminiscent of a binding equation.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing functional scores to catalytic rates.

claim: There is an apparent non-linear relationship between the functional scores measured in both the FRET and TF screens, and the relative catalytic activity of mutants measured independently for Mpro in vitro (R2=0.81 for non-linear fit to TF screen and R2=0.93 for non-linear fit to FRET screen).
source: Using this approach, we observed an apparent non-linear relationship between the functional scores measured in both the FRET and TF screens, and the relative catalytic activity of mutants measured independently for Mpro in vitro in various studies (R2=0.81 for non-linear fit to TF screen and R2=0.93 for non-linear fit to FRET screen) (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a result from fitting the data to different models.

claim: There is a stronger linear relationship (R2=0.86) between the scores measured in the growth screen and the catalytic efficiencies of the individual mutants compared to the fluorescent screens.
source: Compared to the fluorescent screens, there is a stronger linear relationship (R2=0.86) between the scores measured in our growth screen and the catalytic efficiencies of the individual mutants.
evidence: This is a result from comparing different screens to catalytic data.

claim: The growth screen more fully captures the dynamic range of mutations with small functional defects that tend to appear WT-like in the FRET and TF screens.
source: These analyses indicate that the growth screen more fully captures the dynamic range of mutations with small functional defects that tend to appear WT-like in the FRET and TF screens.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of screens.

claim: The vast majority of clinical isolates that have been sequenced to date have either 0 or 1 Mpro mutations with fewer than 0.4% having 2 or more mutations.
source: The vast majority of the clinical isolates that have been sequenced to date have either 0 or 1 Mpro mutations with fewer than 0.4% having 2 or more mutations and thus we did not account for epistasis in our analysis.
evidence: This is an observation from analyzing clinical sequence data.

claim: The most abundant clinical variants are highly functional in the assays.
source: We found that the most abundant clinical variants are highly functional in our assays (Figure 5a [FRET and growth screens] and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a [TF screen]); however, lower frequency variants in clinical samples were found to have a wide range of Mpro function.
evidence: This is a result from analyzing clinical variants.

claim: Lower frequency variants in clinical samples have a wide range of Mpro function.
source: We found that the most abundant clinical variants are highly functional in our assays (Figure 5a [FRET and growth screens] and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a [TF screen]); however, lower frequency variants in clinical samples were found to have a wide range of Mpro function.
evidence: This is a result from analyzing clinical variants.

claim: Mpro sequences among the clinical samples include premature stop codons that have been observed up to 100 times.
source: Surprisingly, Mpro sequences among the clinical samples include premature stop codons that have been observed up to 100 times (out of over 5 million total isolates to date) (Figure 5a [FRET and growth screens] and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a [TF screen]).
evidence: This is an observation from clinical sequence data.

claim: The frequency of stop codons observed in clinical data is assumed to be an indication of sequencing error in the clinical samples.
source: Because Mpro function is required for viral fitness, we assume that the frequency of stop codons observed in the data is an indication of sequencing error in the clinical samples.
evidence: This is an inference based on the essential nature of Mpro.

claim: Among the 290 non-synonymous mutations in the Mpro gene that have been observed more than 100 times, the vast majority exhibit WT-like function with only nine having a score below that of the WT distribution.
source: Accounting for this sequencing error, we examined the functional score of the 290 non-synonymous mutations in the Mpro gene that have been observed more than 100 times. The vast majority of these clinical variants exhibit WT-like function with only nine having a score below that of the WT distribution (see Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing clinical variants.

claim: The observed enrichment for variants with WT-like function in the circulating SARS-CoV-2 virus indicates that Mpro is undergoing strong purifying selection in the human population.
source: This observed enrichment for variants with WT-like function in the circulating SARS-CoV-2 virus indicates that Mpro is undergoing strong purifying selection in the human population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the functional analysis of clinical variants.

claim: There is a 96% sequence identity between the SARS-CoV-2 and the SARS-CoV-1 Mpro proteases, with only 12 amino acid differences.
source: There is a 96% sequence identity between the SARS-CoV-2 and the SARS-CoV-1 Mpro proteases, with only 12 amino acid differences.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence similarity.

claim: All of the amino acid differences in SARS-CoV-1 Mpro are WT-like in SARS-CoV-2 in the screens.
source: In our study, all of the amino acid differences in SARS-CoV-1 Mpro are WT-like in SARS-CoV-2, underscoring the credibility of the functional scores (Figure 5b [FRET and growth screens] and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b [TF screen]).
evidence: This is a result that validates the functional scores.

claim: A set of 852 Mpro homolog sequences with an average homology of 47% from genetically diverse coronaviruses was analyzed.
source: We went on to analyze the diversity in 852 sequences across a set of Mpro homologs with an average homology of 47% from genetically diverse coronaviruses.
evidence: This describes the dataset analyzed for natural variation.

claim: 1207 amino acid changes located at 263 positions of Mpro were identified in the natural homolog sequences.
source: We identified 1207 amino acid changes located at 263 positions of Mpro and examined the functional score of these variants in our data.
evidence: This describes the natural variation found in homologs.

claim: There was enrichment toward functional Mpro variants among natural homologs with only 6% (77 out of 1207) natural variants having functional scores in the FRET screen below the WT range.
source: Here again, we saw enrichment toward functional Mpro variants with only 6% (77 out of 1207) natural variants having functional scores in the FRET screen below the WT range (Figure 5b and Figure 5c [FRET and growth screens] and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b [TF screen]).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing natural variants.

claim: Further analysis of deleterious natural variants should provide insight into the role epistasis played in the historical evolution of Mpro.
source: Further analysis of these deleterious variants should provide insight into the role epistasis played in the historical evolution of Mpro, and these insights may have utility in the generation of future pan-coronavirus inhibitors.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: About 24 positions of Mpro exhibited low mutation tolerance, defined as 17 or more substitutions with null-like function.
source: About 24 positions of Mpro exhibited low mutation tolerance, defined as 17 or more substitutions with null-like function: P9, S10, G11, E14, R40, H41, T111, S113, R131, C145, G146, S147, G149, F150, H163, G174, G179, G183, D187, D197, N203, D289, E290, and D295 (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a result identifying mutation-intolerant positions.

claim: Only four of the mutation-sensitive residues contact the substrate: H41, C145, H163, and D187.
source: Only four of these mutation-sensitive residues contact the substrate: H41 and C145 (the catalytic residues), as well as H163 and D187.
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: H163 interacts with the invariable P1 Gln of the substrate.
source: H163 interacts with the invariable P1 Gln of the substrate and D187 forms a hydrogen bond with a catalytic water and a salt bridge with R40.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of substrate interactions.

claim: D187 forms a hydrogen bond with a catalytic water and a salt bridge with R40.
source: H163 interacts with the invariable P1 Gln of the substrate and D187 forms a hydrogen bond with a catalytic water and a salt bridge with R40.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge.

claim: A large body of work has previously shown that dimerization is indispensable to Mpro function.
source: A large body of work has previously shown that dimerization is indispensable to Mpro function (Chou et al., 2004; Hsu et al., 2005a, Chen et al., 2008; Cheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The study supports the critical functional role of dimerization as there is prevalent mutation-sensitivity in residues at the dimer interface, including P9, S10, G11, E14, and E290.
source: Our study also supports the critical functional role of dimerization as we see prevalent mutation-sensitivity in residues at the dimer interface, including P9, S10, G11, E14, and E290, each of which cannot be altered without complete loss of function.
evidence: This is a result from the functional screens.

claim: Residues P9, S10, G11, E14, and E290 at the dimer interface cannot be altered without complete loss of function.
source: Our study also supports the critical functional role of dimerization as we see prevalent mutation-sensitivity in residues at the dimer interface, including P9, S10, G11, E14, and E290, each of which cannot be altered without complete loss of function.
evidence: This is a result from the functional screens.

claim: R131, D197, N203, D289, and E290 lie at the interface of Domain II and Domain III sandwiched between dimers and make up part of a surface identified by structural modeling as a possible distal drug binding pocket.
source: The R131, D197, N203, D289, and E290 lie at the interface of Domain II and Domain III sandwiched between dimers and make up part of a surface identified by structural modeling as a possible distal drug binding pocket (Bhat et al., 2021; Weng et al., 2021; Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural modeling studies.

claim: A dynamic salt bridge is formed between R131 located on the loop of Domain II connecting β10–11 of the catalytic pocket, and D289 in the α-helical Domain III that has been reported to contribute to the flexibility and structural plasticity of Mpro.
source: Within this cluster, a dynamic salt bridge is formed between R131 located on the loop of Domain II connecting β10–11 of the catalytic pocket, and D289 in the α-helical Domain III that has been reported to contribute to the flexibility and structural plasticity of Mpro (Bhat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: The location of R131, D197, N203, D289, and E290 at the interface of the two domains and the dimer interface, combined with the fact that they are critical to Mpro function suggests that they are part of a distal regulatory communication network.
source: The location of these residues at the interface of the two domains and the dimer interface, combined with the fact that they are critical to Mpro function suggests that they are part of a distal regulatory communication network.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural location and functional importance.

claim: The critical function played by the network of residues R131, D197, N203, D289, and E290 provides motivation for further examination of their potential as a mutation-resistant target for inhibitor design.
source: Our studies clearly indicate the critical function played by this network of residues providing motivation for further examination of their potential as a mutation-resistant target for inhibitor design.
evidence: This is a speculation about future drug design applications.

claim: A second cluster of mutation-intolerant residues appear to be part of an allosteric communication network between the active site and the dimerization interface.
source: A second cluster of mutation-intolerant residues appear to be part of an allosteric communication network between the active site and the dimerization interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural location of mutation-sensitive residues.

claim: Prior studies of individual mutations suggest allosteric connections between the dimerization and active sites.
source: Prior studies of individual mutations also suggest allosteric connections between the dimerization and active sites.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work in the field.

claim: Mutations at both E166 and S147 were found to disrupt dimerization.
source: Mutations at both E166 (Cheng et al., 2010) and S147 (Barrila et al., 2006) were found to disrupt dimerization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both positions E166 and S147 are located distal to the dimerization site, suggesting that the properties of these two sites are interdependent.
source: Both positions E166 and S147 are located distal to the dimerization site, suggesting that the properties of these two sites are interdependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural location and functional effects.

claim: There is a physically interacting chain of mutation-sensitive residues that bridge from the active site to the dimerization site composed of H163, S147, L115, and S10.
source: Our results show that there is a physically interacting chain of mutation-sensitive residues that bridge from the active site to the dimerization site (Figure 6c). This bridge is composed of H163 that directly contacts the P1 Gln of substrate, S147, L115, and S10 at the dimer interface.
evidence: This is a result from structural and functional analysis.

claim: Each of the dimer-to-active site bridging residues H163, S147, L115, and S10 are critical to Mpro function and are strongly conserved among Mpro homologs.
source: Each of these dimer-to-active site bridging residues are critical to Mpro function and are strongly conserved among Mpro homologs.
evidence: This is a result from functional and evolutionary analysis.

claim: The physical interactions between H163, S147, L115, and S10 mediate critical communication between the active sites of both subunits in the Mpro dimer.
source: Based on these observations, we suggest that the physical interactions between H163, S147, L115, and S10 mediate critical communication between the active sites of both subunits in the Mpro dimer.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional data.

claim: All 24 of the identified mutation-intolerant residues are highly conserved among SARS-CoV-2 Mpro homologs.
source: All 24 of the identified mutation-intolerant residues are highly conserved among SARS-CoV-2 Mpro homologs (Figure 6d [FRET and growth screens] and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 [TF screen]).
evidence: This is a result from evolutionary analysis.

claim: While functional hot spots accurately predict evolutionary conservation, conservation does not accurately predict functional hot spots.
source: While functional hot spots accurately predict evolutionary conservation, conservation does not accurately predict functional hot spots.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing functional and evolutionary data.

claim: There are many residues in Mpro that are strongly conserved, but that can be mutated without strong impacts on function.
source: There are many residues in Mpro that are strongly conserved, but that can be mutated without strong impacts on function.
evidence: This is a result from comparing functional and evolutionary data.

claim: The pattern where conservation does not accurately predict functional hot spots has been widely observed for other proteins.
source: This pattern has been widely observed for other proteins (Hietpas et al., 2011; Melamed et al., 2013; Roscoe et al., 2013; Starita et al., 2013; Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on other proteins.

claim: One of the outstanding differences between natural evolution and experimental studies of fitness is the strength of selection.
source: While many features distinguish natural evolution and experimental studies of fitness (Boucher et al., 2019) one of the outstanding differences is the strength of selection.
evidence: This is supported by citation and reflects understanding of evolutionary theory.

claim: Small fitness changes that may be too small for experimental resolution can drive selection in natural evolution due to large population sizes and timescales.
source: While functional hot spots can be defined by strong impacts on function that are experimentally measurable, small fitness changes that may be too small for experimental resolution can drive selection in natural evolution due to large population sizes and timescales (Ohta, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to evolutionary theory.

claim: The functional screen captures the mutations that are critical to catalytic function while evolutionary conservation depicts a wide range of mutations including those that make more nuanced contributions to function.
source: Our functional screen captures the mutations that are critical to catalytic function while evolutionary conservation depicts a wide range of mutations including those that make more nuanced contributions to function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences between functional and evolutionary data.

claim: When designing drugs to disrupt Mpro function, it will be important to focus on the functionally critical sites which are a subset of the evolutionarily conserved positions.
source: When designing drugs to disrupt Mpro function, we hypothesize that it will be important to focus on the functionally critical sites which are a subset of the evolutionarily conserved positions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about drug design strategy.

claim: The active site is the target binding site for most inhibitors that have been generated against Mpro.
source: We focused these analyses on the active site, which is the target binding site for most inhibitors that have been generated against Mpro (Cho et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of inhibitors.

claim: There is dramatic variability in mutational sensitivity at substrate-contact positions.
source: In our functional screens, we found dramatic variability in mutational sensitivity at these substrate-contact positions.
evidence: This is a result from the functional screens.

claim: Residues G143, H163, D187, and Q192 were extremely sensitive to mutation.
source: For example, residues G143, H163, D187, and Q192 were extremely sensitive to mutation, while residues M49, N142, E166, and Q189 were highly tolerant.
evidence: This is a result from the functional screens.

claim: Residues M49, N142, E166, and Q189 were highly tolerant to mutation.
source: For example, residues G143, H163, D187, and Q192 were extremely sensitive to mutation, while residues M49, N142, E166, and Q189 were highly tolerant.
evidence: This is a result from the functional screens.

claim: Despite the diverse sequence variation amongst Mpro's substrates, they occupy a conserved volume in the active site, known as the substrate envelope.
source: Despite the diverse sequence variation amongst Mpro's substrates, they occupy a conserved volume in the active site, known as the substrate envelope, and the interactions between Mpro's residues and all of its substrates are highly conserved (Shaqra et al., 2022) indicating that our mutation results from the Nsp4/5 cut-site will likely translate to other cut-sites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural work.

claim: The interactions between Mpro's residues and all of its substrates are highly conserved.
source: Despite the diverse sequence variation amongst Mpro's substrates, they occupy a conserved volume in the active site, known as the substrate envelope, and the interactions between Mpro's residues and all of its substrates are highly conserved (Shaqra et al., 2022) indicating that our mutation results from the Nsp4/5 cut-site will likely translate to other cut-sites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural work.

claim: The mutation results from the Nsp4/5 cut-site will likely translate to other cut-sites.
source: Despite the diverse sequence variation amongst Mpro's substrates, they occupy a conserved volume in the active site, known as the substrate envelope, and the interactions between Mpro's residues and all of its substrates are highly conserved (Shaqra et al., 2022) indicating that our mutation results from the Nsp4/5 cut-site will likely translate to other cut-sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conserved substrate envelope.

claim: N142, E166, and Q189 are positions whose side chains make direct hydrogen bonds with substrates that are surprisingly tolerant to mutation.
source: Even among residues whose side chains make direct hydrogen bonds with substrates are positions that are surprisingly tolerant to mutation, namely N142, E166, and Q189.
evidence: This is a result from the functional screens.

claim: N142 forms distinct hydrogen bonds with Nsp4/5 and Nsp8/9, which has been proposed as a mechanism of Mpro substrate recognition.
source: N142 forms distinct hydrogen bonds with Nsp4/5 and Nsp8/9, which has been proposed as a mechanism of Mpro substrate recognition (MacDonald et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Q189 is in a flexible loop that closes over the substrates, allowing accommodation of diverse cut-sites.
source: Q189 is in a flexible loop that closes over the substrates, allowing accommodation of diverse cut-sites (Shaqra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural work.

claim: The proposed substrate-recognition positions N142, E166, and Q189 are very tolerant to mutation and have high potential for developing inhibitor resistance.
source: In our screens, we find that these proposed substrate-recognition positions are very tolerant to mutation (Figure 7b [FRET and growth screens] and Figure 7—figure supplement 1b [TF screen]) and have high potential for developing inhibitor resistance.
evidence: This is a result and inference from the functional screens.

claim: Mutations at N142, E166, and Q189 are compatible with function and are readily available to the evolution of drug resistance.
source: Our results indicate that mutations at N142, E166, and Q189 are compatible with function and are readily available to the evolution of drug resistance.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional data.

claim: A recent study comprehensively examined 233 X-ray crystal structures of SARS-CoV-2 Mpro in complex with a wide range of inhibitors.
source: A recent study comprehensively examined 233 X-ray crystal structures of SARS-CoV-2 Mpro in complex with a wide range of inhibitors (Cho et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comprehensive structural study.

claim: In 185 of 233 Mpro-inhibitor structures, inhibitors lie in the same binding pocket in the active site, primarily contacting Mpro positions T25, H41, M49, N142, S144, C145, H163, H164, E166, P168, H172, Q189, and A191.
source: In 185 of these 233 structures, inhibitors lie in the same binding pocket in the active site, primarily contacting Mpro positions T25, H41, M49, N142, S144, C145, H163, H164, E166, P168, H172, Q189, and A191.
evidence: This is based on analysis of structural data cited.

claim: Residues N142, E166, and Q189 form direct hydrogen bonds with many Mpro inhibitors and most mutations at these positions result in a functional protease.
source: Of note, residues N142, E166, and Q189 form direct hydrogen bonds with many Mpro inhibitors and most mutations at these positions result in a functional protease.
evidence: This combines structural knowledge with functional data from the screens.

claim: T25, M49, M164, P168, and A191 form van der Waals interactions with a variety of inhibitors suggesting that mutations at these positions could disrupt inhibitor interactions while maintaining Mpro function.
source: Additionally, T25, M49, M164, P168, and A191 form van der Waals interactions with a variety of inhibitors suggesting that mutations at these positions could disrupt inhibitor interactions while maintaining Mpro function.
evidence: This is an inference combining structural knowledge with functional data.

claim: Positions H41, S144, C145, H163, and H172 are highly sensitive in the screens, as well as strongly conserved in nature, and therefore would be ideal contact positions for inhibitors with reduced likelihood of evolving Mpro resistance.
source: In contrast, positions H41, S144, C145, H163, and H172 are highly sensitive in our screen, as well as strongly conserved in nature, and therefore would be ideal contact positions for inhibitors with reduced likelihood of evolving Mpro resistance.
evidence: This is an inference about drug design based on functional and evolutionary data.

claim: Pfizer has developed the first FDA-authorized Mpro inhibitor, PF-07321332.
source: Pfizer has developed the first FDA-authorized Mpro inhibitor, PF-07321332 (Owen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a factual statement supported by citation.

claim: Evolutionarily accessible resistance mutations are single base change mutations that would disrupt inhibitor binding while maintaining WT-like substrate recognition and cleavage.
source: Evolutionarily accessible resistance mutations are single base change mutations that would disrupt inhibitor binding while maintaining WT-like substrate recognition and cleavage.
evidence: This defines the criteria used to identify potential resistance mutations.

claim: Three mutations, Q189E, E166A, and E166Q, were identified with potential resistance against PF-07321332.
source: These criteria led to the identification of three mutations, Q189E, E166A, and E166Q with potential resistance against PF-07321332.
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the structure and functional data.

claim: The three positions Q189, E166 are at sites where the inhibitor PF-07321332 protrudes out of the defined substrate envelope.
source: These three positions are at sites where the inhibitor protrudes out of the defined substrate envelope, providing further evidence that these residues may evolve inhibitor resistance while maintaining substrate recognition (Shaqra et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural work on the substrate envelope.

claim: Q189E is a natural variant in both the avian infectious bronchitis virus and the swine coronavirus, HKU15 CoV.
source: Of note, Q189E is a natural variant in both the avian infectious bronchitis virus and the swine coronavirus, HKU15 CoV, widely detected in pigs in Asia and North America and of pandemic concern due to its ability to replicate in human cells (Edwards et al., 2020).
